title: Farmers blindsided by approval of 155-turbine wind farm ahead of election
text:
The Victorian government has signed off on a large wind and battery project for the state's north, on the eve of entering caretaker mode ahead of this month's state election.

Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny signed off on a planning permit for the Meering West Wind Farm on Monday, just a day before the caretaker period came into effect.

The facility to be built at Meering West, about 140km north-west of Bendigo, would be one of Australia's largest, incorporating up to 155 wind turbines.

Construction on the project, which would deliver 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity and 1,000 megawatt-hours of battery energy storage, is due to start in 2029.

Like other similar facilities, it has been deeply controversial among local residents, with many farmers rallying against its approval.

The timing of the approval is further complicated by the facility's intention to tap into the VNI West transmission line, which is yet to be built and would be scrapped if the Victorian Coalition came to government.

Vocal critics 'not heard'

Tyler Nelson is one of many neighbouring farmers who have objected to the project.

He said he was not surprised the government had signed off on it at the last minute.

"I'm very disappointed, but at the same time I can't say I'm shocked with the behaviour of the Labor government," he said.

"It's well established that there are a lot of projects being rushed through at the 11th hour and there's been a pretty poor process involved for quite some time."

Tyler Nelson is among the many farmers who oppose the Meering West wind farm. (Supplied: Tyler Nelson)

Mr Nelson said he and other neighbours had been unaware of the project until it was well advanced.

"Most neighbours and those affected found out pretty late in the piece, once there were contracts and caveats in place," he said.

" We were kept in the dark for quite some time and were trying to play catch-up in terms of what it all means for us. "

Mr Nelson said more than 100 people had objected to the project, with concerns including noise, shadow, flicker, land devaluation, fire risk and impacts on the natural environment.

He said their objections and requests, including removing turbines from the project footprint close to objecting neighbours, had not been adopted.

The wind farm at Meering West would have 1.3 gigawatts of generation capacity. (Supplied: Pixabay/JACLOU-DL/License/File)

A community divided

Mr Nelson was reluctant to comment on the community divisions the project had created.

"I've tried not to let it affect me, but it's difficult not to," he said.

"Communities that usually stand together and talk, when that's taken away, it seems a bit odd."

Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

Given the Coalition has committed to scrap VNI West, Mr Nelson said he hoped there would be a change of government on November 28, but he was not convinced it would leave the Meering West project dead in the water.

"It would be nice to think that is the case, but what we're learning is we never know what's happening with backroom deals," he said.

"Yes, scrapping VNI West is a good move by the Coalition, but what does it mean for this project?

"It's my understanding that [project proponent Virya] will continue to develop on somehow, but I don't know what that looks like."

The Victorian government, Meering West Wind Farm representatives and developer Virya were contacted for comment.

title: Backup World Cup wheelchair travels across the world in stranger's luggage
text:
An Irish tourist visiting Australia has helped deliver a specialist replacement wheelchair to her national rugby league team, hours before it was needed.

Irish wheelchair rugby league player Oran Spain snapped his wheelchair last week while training in Wollongong, where the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup is being staged.

Irish wheelchair rugby league player Oran Spain says he has been training for four years to be selected in his national side. (Supplied: Rugby League Ireland)

Being much smaller than his teammates, the only other wheelchair in the world tailored for the 20-year-old was in Ireland.

At age two, he was diagnosed with XLP, a rare, life-threatening generic immunodeficiency disorder.

"We knew we had a chair at home so my family went on a mission to see if we could get the chair to Sydney," team manager and Oran's mother Susan Spain said.

Public radio call-out

Oran's uncle Austin Smith called RTE radio, Ireland's national public broadcaster, to put the call out for someone to help transport the chair to Australia.

Deirdre Donoghue was listening and called the radio station.

"I thought 'are they talking to me or am I hearing things'?

Deirdre Donoghue departs Ireland with Oran Spain's replacement wheelchair alongside members of Oran's family. (Supplied: Jim Marshall)

"I didn't know if anyone else was going to ring in so I thought I'd ring in and see if I can help out.

"I was coming out anyway to meet my friend who I haven't seen for 10 years and I heard the request on the radio on Friday and I was heading out Sunday.

"It [the wheelchair] was transferred to all my connecting flights so I didn't have to think about it — it was grand bringing it over and I thought it was important to bring it over to help out."

Deirdre Donoghue was met by Susan and Oran Spain at Sydney Airport today. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Wheelchair safely delivered in Sydney

Oran and Susan Spain were at Sydney International Airport today to meet Deirdre and collect the precious wheelchair.

"It's incredible, this gives me the opportunity to play," Oran said.

"I've been working on this for four years trying to get to a World Cup to be selected — I've been flying over to Wigan in England to play every weekend in the summer and now Deirdre's given me the opportunity to achieve that dream.

"When I was a boy I wanted to play the running game and my only goal was to play for my country, so when I went into the wheelchair that goal shifted a little, but I wouldn't have it any other way.

" It's incredible to put on that green shirt. "

Oran Spain had his cracked wheelchair welded after the training accident but decided not to use it in a game due to safety concerns. (Supplied: Jim Marshall)

What makes the wheelchairs so special?

Rugby league wheelchairs are not only tailored to the body of the athlete, they are designed for the speed and high impact of the sport.

Chairs usually cost between $4,000 and $9,000, while Australian wheelchair rugby league captain Bayley McKenna's chair cost $15,000.

"They're incredibly specialised and my broken wheelchair was tailored to me and this one Deirdre's brought over is too," Oran Spain said.

"The wheels are angled, the front bars are rounded for contact and I'm a bit smaller than my teammates, so none of their chairs would work.

"There are not many chairs that would work in the world [for me]."

Ireland's Oran Spain appeared energetic in his replacement wheelchair while warming up for his game against Wales. (ABC Illawarra: Brooke Chandler)

Ready to take the court

With his replacement wheelchair now in Wollongong, Oran Spain rolled out with his teammates for the first time after missing his side's opening World Cup match against the USA last Friday.

Ireland won that game 110-10.

Susan Spain said Oran's presence in the team is a significant moment for her family and the team.

"For him to be able to compete and do something he’s been training for and we’ve all been invested in for all these years is huge," she said.

" When the chair broke, the devastation on Oran's face alone told me this was something that couldn't be fixed. "

The family tried to have the wheelchair welded after the incident, but decided not to risk using it because the weld may not have held and another impact could crack it again.

The Spain family presented Deirdre Donoghue with match tickets, an official team polo shirt, hat and pennant which the side exchanges with other teams before a game.

Ms Donoghue said her holiday will now incorporate a trip to Wollongong to watch her national side in action.

"I've got the tickets and a jersey now so I'll have to go and see what it's like," she said.

title: Tough Christmas looms as rates and inflation hit household budgets
text:
Bah, humbug!

In a split decision, the nine members of Australia's Reserve Bank's board have decided to deliver Australia's highly-indebted households a fifth — but hopefully final — interest rate hike for 2026.

The board will meet again on December 7 and 8, but any future hikes are more likely to be delivered in the new year.

But it won't be an easy Christmas.

RBA interest rate updates: Follow coverage to today's interest rate decision, plus market reaction and analysis on our live blog.

Official forecasts released by the RBA on Tuesday show workers can expect their real pay packets to shrink this financial year, with wages rising just 3.4 per cent compared to a forecast 3.7 per cent rise in prices.

And we'll end the calendar year with a headline inflation rate of 4.5 per cent — well above the RBA's target of 2 to 3 per cent, revised up from a previous forecast of 3.6 per cent compiled only three months ago.

Higher oil prices, along with stronger-than-anticipated price pressures at home, have the Reserve Bank thinking it will not get inflation back to within its target band of between 2 and 3 per cent until the second half of next year.

It's a gloomy picture for households.

Mortgages eating up disposable income

Mortgage minimum repayments are were already eating up 10 per cent of household disposable income ahead of this week's decision, figures from the Reserve Bank's Statement on Monetary Policy show.

Once the full effect of September's and this week's rate hikes are factored into repayments, Aussie home loan payments will be sitting at the highest level since the pre-Global Financial Crisis period in late 2007 and 2008.

Indeed, visions of 2008 — the last time interest rates were this high — now dance in our heads.

If you remember, mortgage holders began 2008 under a freshly elected Rudd government and groaning under the weight of high interest rates.

The Reserve Bank, then under Glenn Stevens, ratcheted up interest rates to try to dampen the inflationary pressures created by a Chinese-fuelled boom in Australian commodity export prices.

Who's to blame for interest rate hikes? The coalition has been blaming federal government spending for rising inflation and another impending rate rise for Melbourne Cup Day, but the figures tell a different story.

This filled government coffers with cash, which in turn was funnelled to households via successive annual tax cuts.

Back then it was prime ministerial hopeful Kevin Rudd lambasting the Howard and Costello government and declaring "this reckless spending must stop". His future treasurer Wayne Swan would go on to declare that the previous government had "let the inflation genie out of the bottle".

Same game, different colours.

Australian economy looks different now

The economic landscape today is very different, however, to those pre-GFC mining boom days.

The Australian economy has already cooled and expected to grow by a meagre 1.6 per cent this year, slowing to 1.3 per cent next year.

The magnitude of house price falls has surprised even the Reserve Bank, which notes the impact of both higher interest rates and recent tax changes.

Much of the inflationary pressure today is not explained by a run-away strong economy, but rolling external price shocks, most notably for oil, which the RBA fears are becoming increasingly entrenched in people's expectations for future price rises.

Loading

It's not just about mortgages

So, will a strategy of crunching borrowers work to bring price pressures to heel?

Well, the RBA is keen to let you know that crunching borrowers' cash flow is only one of four major "channels" through which higher interest rates work — and the least potent at that.

There's also the exchange rate effect by which the Aussie dollar is bolstered compared to other countries, which, in turn, makes imported goods less expensive.

Loading...

Then there is the "inter-temporal substitution" channel, which is a fancy way to say that higher interest rates encourage people to save more and borrow less, dampening demand.

Added to that is home owners the "wealth effect" whereby higher interest rates contribute to lower house prices than otherwise, just generally making homeowners (including those with no mortgage) feel less rich.

It's a calculated strategy to cool the rising cost of living — albeit one which will fall most heavily on the shoulders of Australian mortgage holders.

Will it work? We're about to find out.

title: Despair turns to hope for single mum on house hunting mission
text:
After years of searching for a home as Perth property prices continued to rise at an unprecedented rate, Vanessa Bray finally feels like she has a fighting chance of securing one.

The single mum has been buoyed by new figures showing Australia is tracking towards its biggest housing market downturn in 40 years, with Perth's house prices dropping 5.7 per cent over the last three months.

Data from property research group Cotality shows Perth's median dwelling price has fallen to $942,018 — a drop of nearly $100,000 since peaking at more than $1 million in April.

Meanwhile, economists at the Commonwealth Bank today released an updated forecast predicting Perth property prices would plummet 18 per cent from that April peak, before prices begin to stabilise in the second half of 2027.

Hope on the horizon

For Ms Bray, the easing market spells hope of finding a home for her and her sons.

Vanessa Bray is feeling a lot more positive about buying a home in light of recent data. (ABC News: Madigan Landry)

"I can't even begin to describe the relief that I feel for myself and my kids that we could maybe have a home of our own," she said.

"It's close. I feel like it will happen instead of the despair that I had that it was never going to happen."

Australia's property downturn National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, according to property research group Cotality.

Ms Bray has been looking for a family home since she and her partner separated four years ago.

She needs to find something in their school catchment while staying under the $850,000 cap needed to qualify for the state government's Help to Buy Scheme.

Ms Bray said her experience of trying to buy a home had been '"devastating" and like being on a "rollercoaster".

"[I've gone from] thinking, 'right, this could finally be it. I'm going to make it. I'm going to have long-term security for me and my kids' to the devastation of 'I've missed out again'," she said.

"It was a really tough time."

Perth's median dwelling price has fallen by almost $100,000 in six months. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

Too optimistic, too soon

While the recent slump in prices represents a glimmer of hope for those trying to break into the market, the softening represents a small dent in the meteoric rise in Perth's property prices, which have risen 93 per cent in a decade, including 68 per cent in the last five years.

Perth realtor Kyle Peters warned the optimism of those trying to enter the market could be premature.

Mr Peters said the recent figures were not a good representation of the true state of Australia's housing market.

"It would be an interesting anomaly that a housing market would crash when we have a housing crisis and don't have enough houses for people to live in," Mr Peters said.

"At the rate things were ramping up before, there needed to be some abatement, but certainly we [still] have a housing shortage."

Buyers can be more selective

REIWA president Rob Mandanici said even if prices did not continue to fall on the same trajectory, the slowing market still provided benefits for those entering the market.

REIWA President Rob Mandanici says the easing should give buyers some breathing space. (ABC News: Madigan Landry)

"They can take a little bit more time to make that purchasing decision and not feel that immense pressure to rush into a decision," he said.

"The buyers themselves haven't disappeared, they've become more selective."

House prices are falling all around the country. (ABC News: Charlotte Wilkes )

Mr Mandanici said there was no doubt Australia was experiencing "a little bit of a market slowdown", but said the dip in prices did not amount to a crash.

"We are seeing some prices across multiple Perth suburbs pull back, but a lot of those suburbs are coming off highs," he said.

"We've got a lot of buyers sitting on the sidelines and I think today's interest rate decision will just give buyers the certainty that they want moving forward."

On Tuesday the Reserve Bank increased interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, lifting the cash rate to 4.85 per cent, the highest it has been since 2008.

title: 'He was surrounded by love': One year of voluntary assisted dying in the ACT
text:
This time last year, Anthea Smith picked up the phone to get her husband access to voluntary assisted dying.

The pair were high school sweethearts and had been together for more than three decades.

"Jason was a bit of a larrikin. He was very cheeky. We grew up in rural New South Wales together and we met at school," Jason's wife Anthea said.

After battling motor neuron disease for eight years, Jason was the first person to apply for voluntary assisted dying in the ACT when it came into effect a year ago today.

Jason and Anthea Smith were high school sweethearts. (Supplied)

"Jason didn't want to have a long palliative sedation death; he wanted to go quickly, and so we were the first family to actually ring the care navigator service on the 3rd of November in 2025," she said.

"I'm so grateful that voluntary assisted dying was available to us.

"Because Jason had lived with motor neuron disease for nearly nine years, at that stage we were actually grateful, and that might sound a little bit unusual, but we'd already started the grieving process as Jason was losing functionality as his body was giving way."

When Jason died in June this year by voluntary assisted dying, he was surrounded by his family and carers, in his home where he was most comfortable.

"It was obviously a very emotional day, but we actually had lots of laughs and lots of tears," Ms Smith said.

"He was surrounded by love."

She said that while learning to live without Jason was tough, it was made easier knowing he had a peaceful death.

"It wasn't traumatic," she said.

"We knew he was at end of life, and he died really peacefully".

Loading...

More than 50 people have died through scheme

The Voluntary Assisted Dying Oversight Board released its inaugural report today and found that 57 people had chosen to end their lives through the program.

The data was gathered between November 3, 2025, and June 30, 2026.

During this time period, more than 150 people requested the scheme, with 110 of those people having reached the final request stage.

Gail wants the choice to 'die with dignity'. Now she can Canberrans like Gail Ford are now able to apply for the ACT's new voluntary assisted dying scheme, which its advocates say gives dignity in death to applicants.

The median period between a first request and death was 20 days, and the median age of people making an enquiry was 77.

ACT Voluntary Assisted Dying Oversight Board chair Darlene Cox said the board had reviewed every case so far and had found no major issues.

"We haven't identified any systemic safety concerns, and we think the legislative safeguards have been operating as intended," she said.

'Most progressive' program in country: minister

In June 2024, the ACT Legislative Assembly voted to make voluntary assisted dying legal in the territory, becoming one of the last Australian jurisdictions to do so.

The scheme came into effect exactly a year ago today.

The ACT government has heralded the territory's framework as the "most progressive" in the country.

Health Minister Marisa Paterson said those using the program had "been able to end their lives with dignity and autonomy, at the right time for them".

ACT Health Minister Marisa Paterson says she is proud of the territory's voluntary assisted dying framework. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

The minister said the framework "leads the way nationally in terms of not having a time frame to death required. There's no mandated time frames between steps of the scheme".

The territory government has called on the federal government to extend their legislation and repeal the Commonwealth Criminal Code to allow telehealth consults for voluntary assisted dying.

The community will be able to provide feedback on the program when a review is carried out in 2028.

title: Star trainer Maher claims second Melbourne Cup as Point of Law storms to win
text:
Point of Law has given trainer Ciaron Maher his second Melbourne Cup victory.

The Geelong Cup-winner maintained his form, becoming the third Northern Hemisphere three-year-old to win after Rekindling in 2017 and Cross Counter in 2018.

The horse, making the sixth start of his career, ran down stablemate Royal Supremacy in the straight to win an incredible race, beating Zahrann and Juja Kibo also from the Maher stable.

This gave Maher the Cup trifecta.

Ethan Brown rode Point of Law, formerly owned by King Charles III and Queen Camilla, to victory, winning his first Melbourne Cup.

In a dramatic race, Royal Supremacy hit the front in the first half of the race and in a brave effort, went all-out for the lead, stretching the margin to up to 20 lengths by the 1,000m mark.

As the rest of the field scrambled to rein in the leader, Royal Supremacy maintained a huge gap around the turn and into the long Flemington straight.

For a time it looked like he would win, with Royal Supremacy still a thumping 12 lengths clear at the 400m. But Brown pushed Point of Law out of the chasing pack to produce an incredible finishing burst, hitting the front and winning by 3.75 lengths.

Maher was left to ponder the result afterwards.

"I certainly didn't know Royal Supremacy was going to lead by that far but there's nothing better than a true staying test," he said on Channel Nine.

"Point Of Law has just thrived and I can't thank all the team and the owners enough.

"What a ride they've been on. It's been a whirlwind really, but I'm very proud of all the team.

"To get three horses in the first three spots, I'm very proud."

After the race Brown, who is engaged to fellow jockey Celine Gaudray, paid tribute to Maher.

"He took me out of horse training at one stage when I was about 22 years old. But yeah, he's done nothing but support me and backed me and I buggered up plenty of times on his horses and … he's had nothing but faith," he told Channel Nine.

By the time he stepped up to receive his trophy at the presentation, Brown was struggling to come to terms with what had happened.

"I've got to pinch myself here," he said.

There was plenty of emotion as jockey Ethan Brown thanked trainer Ciaron Maher for backing him after their Melbourne Cup win with Point of Law. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

For Maher, it was a peerless Cup training performance. Of his seven Cup runners, he had the trifecta, plus Royal Supremacy hung on to finish fifth, with Shockletz one further back in sixth.

Only Mr Monaco struggled to run out the race, finishing 17th.

It was the first time in 166 editions of the race that the same trainer was responsible for the first three runners home in the Cup.

Irish trainer Joseph O'Brien missed out on a third Cup win with his five entries.

Sons And Lovers, ridden by Dylan Browne McMonagle, was the best finisher in fourth place.

James J Braddock, ridden by Craig Williams, came from the outside barrier and ran home for seventh. Trustyourinstinct, ridden by James McDonald finished 11th, while Kizlyar raced wide for much of the race to get near the front before fading to 16th.

Goodie Two Shoes, ridden by Wayne Lordan, who finished second in last year's race, came second last in 2025.

title: Socceroos, Matildas take Football Australia to court
text:
Socceroos and Matildas stars are taking legal action against Football Australia (FA) as part of a multi-million-dollar dispute between the governing body and its national team players.

AAP understands the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), is pursuing FA for a seven-figure claim on behalf of the players in the NSW Supreme Court.

The union is expected to argue the revenue share agreement between the governing body and national team players is not being serviced properly.

In a statement, FA said it was aware of the PFA's NSW Supreme Court legal action, which the governing body claimed was related to "a third party in connection with a separate matter currently being conducted before the National Dispute Resolution Chamber (NDRC)".

"The Supreme Court's role is limited to the subpoena process, and its involvement ends once that process is complete," an FA spokesperson said.

"As the NDRC matter is ongoing and subject to confidentiality obligations, Football Australia will not comment further."

The PFA declined to comment.

The central issue is believed to centre on FA's commercial deals and whether players are getting a fair share of FA revenues.

As part of the existing collective bargaining agreement (CBA), which was signed in 2023, Socceroos and Matildas players receive a share of FA's national team revenues.

The central issue is believed to be the FA's commercial deals and whether players are getting a fair share of FA revenues. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Registration fees or sponsors for junior participation programs are strictly off-limits to senior national team players.

But anything relating to the Socceroos and Matildas, such as ticketing, broadcast or sponsorship, makes its way back into players' pockets.

National teams contribute up to half of FA's revenues, with players receiving an 18 to 20 per cent cut of all relevant commercial arrangements.

There are also mechanisms in the pay agreement that incentivise players and FA to work together and push for more, allowing both sides to share the spoils of stronger deals.

But the players feel they are not getting their fair share, with the PFA launching legal action in the NSW Supreme Court on their behalf.

String of legal actions against FA

The dispute is the latest high-profile legal action against FA, which settled out of court with Macarthur FC over claims the club was misled by the governing body in the lead-up to its A-League entry in 2020.

FA also recently settled an unfair dismissal case with former chief football officer Ernie Merrick.

The legal dispute with players comes ahead of Socceroos matches in the Middle East during the November window, where tensions are expected to be heightened by the conflict in the region.

Tony Popovic is expected to name his squad later this week to travel to Doha to face Qatar before tackling Jordan in Amman amid a backdrop of increased security concerns.

The Matildas will host Colombia in a two-friendly series in Canberra and Geelong later this month.

The Matildas beat Haiti 7–1 in October. (Getty Images: Football Australia/Catherine Steenkeste)

And the ill-feeling between the players and the governing body comes in the lead-up to the expiry of the current CBA, which is due to lapse in September next year.

Talks are yet to commence over new terms, following an impasse between the PFA and the A-Leagues over a pay deal earlier this year.

AAP

title: What another rate hike means for your mortgage, savings and travel
text:
For the fifth time this year, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has raised the cash rate by 0.25 percentage points as it continues its efforts to curb inflation.

While the effects of RBA rate decisions are most obvious in mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans.

Here's a look at how the latest increase is likely to affect households, whether they're paying off a mortgage, renting, or relying on savings.

Where does the cash rate stand now?

Before looking at who wins and loses from a rate rise, it's worth understanding what the cash rate actually is.

Set by the RBA, the cash rate is Australia's official interest rate charged on unsecured overnight loans between banks.

Put simply, it's how much it costs banks to borrow from each other. When the RBA lifts the cash rate, it becomes more expensive for lenders to borrow from one another.

To offset those higher costs, banks often look at charging customers a higher interest rate to still make a profit because they are paying more to borrow the money in the first place.

On Tuesday, the RBA increased the cash rate to 4.85 per cent to slow down inflation in the economy. The last time the rate was above this level was 18 years ago in November 2008.

PRD chief economist Diaswati Mardiasmo says the central bank has lost its patience, given inflation is on an increasing pattern.

"The theory is, a higher cash rate translates into higher interest rates and mortgage repayments, which dampens household spending on other things like recreation and culture, transport, entertainment, and services," Dr Mardiasmo says.

"As demand/spending goes down, prices of the items also go down, which slows inflation overall."

But that doesn't always work when there are other things in play.

As an example, Dr Mardiasmo points to the war in the Middle East causing fuel prices to increase.

"So even if we don't go out to eat at restaurants as much due to paying for higher mortgage loans, we still have to pay for much more expensive fuel," she says.

Headline inflation rose to 4.3 per cent in the year to September, up from 4.0 per cent in August.

Trimmed mean inflation, the RBA's preferred measure of underlying inflation, rose to an annual rate of 3.6 per cent.

This means underlying inflation has sat above the RBA's 2 to 3 per cent target range for 14 consecutive months.

How the cash rate increase could affect you

Mortgages Read more Read more Rate rises are felt fastest, and most sharply, by Australians with variable-rate mortgages because banks typically pass on RBA increases in full. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver says the cash rate is the main tool steering borrowing costs and households should expect lenders to adjust quickly. "As we've seen with the first four hikes this year, the banks will likely announce a 0.25 per cent increase in their mortgage rates on the same day," Dr Oliver says. Each 0.25 per cent rise in the cash rate adds roughly $92 per month to repayments on a $600,000 variable-rate loan with 25 years remaining. The five 2026 increases totalling 1 per cent have added approximately $456 per month for borrowers on a $600,000 loan. That equates to around $5,472 extra per year. Here's how much a November rate hike will cost borrowers: It is not just existing mortgage borrowers hit by the rate rises though. For prospective buyers, Canstar estimates the borrowing capacity of someone on an average full-time wage of $108,650 would be reduced by more than $58,000, while a couple, both on average wages, would see a reduction of nearly $117,000. If you are on a fixed-rate home loan, you won't see any changes. Those rates are locked in. But when the fixed term expires and rolls to a variable rate, the full impact of any rate cycle will apply at once. Rent Read more Read more For renters, the interest rate impact is more indirect. Some landlords may try to offset the impact of rate rises on their cash flow by increasing rent. Although, there are constraints in how often and how much rent can be increased by each year in most states. But the notion that landlords pass their increased borrowing costs onto renters has been challenged by the RBA. Speaking on 9Now's The Pay Off podcast, RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter said what was really driving rent came down to supply and demand. "If you're an individual landlord, you own one property in one rental market, you might want to put the rent up when your interest rate goes up if you've got a mortgage," Dr Hunter said. "But you're competing with all the other properties that are available … and so, it's demand and supply, it's the local market that will equilibrate rent. "If rents are tracking up, it's usually because demand growth is stronger than supply growth." Cotality's quarterly rental review found rents rose by 0.5 per cent nationally in the September quarter, driven by a severe lack of available stock across the country. The national dwelling vacancy rate sat at 2.1 per cent, unchanged from March and remains well below the pre-COVID decade average of 3.3 per cent. Dr Mardiasmo says higher interest rates can still influence rents indirectly by affecting the number of investors entering the market. "If investors are discouraged from entering the market because of reduced borrowing power and higher loan repayments, there may be fewer rental properties available," Dr Mardiasmo said. "When demand for rental housing remains strong but supply falls, competition among tenants increases and that can put upward pressure on rents." Australian dollar Read more Read more Higher interest rates tend to strengthen the Australian dollar (AUD). And that's because it's more attractive for foreign investors to park their money in Australian interest-bearing assets (like savings accounts, term deposits, and government bonds) because they can get a higher rate of interest here. This increases demand for the AUD, making the currency more valuable. "Australians who are purchasing items overseas, are going on holidays, or have term deposits/savings overseas can benefit," Dr Mardiasmo says. "For businesses who import goods, it also means that their import costs are now cheaper, which supports better profit." But Commonwealth Bank head of Australian economics Belinda Allen says the Australian dollar's value depends on far more than the RBA's cash rate decisions. "The Australian dollar is influenced by many things: global interest rates, commodity prices, China, investor sentiment and expectations about the Australian economy; so you can't say that a 25-basis-point rate hike will automatically result in a particular move in the dollar." Savings and term deposits Read more Read more There is one silver lining: savings account and term deposit interest rates usually rise after an RBA hike, making it more attractive to park your money. This is because, while the cash rate affects borrowing costs for banks, it also sets the rate of return for their own deposits. Cash rate hikes improve their returns, which may be passed on to consumers through higher savings interest rates. Dr Oliver says while short-term deposit rates largely move in line with the cash rate, longer-term term deposit rates are also shaped by government bond yields and other borrowing costs. With today's RBA increase and bond yields already rising, he says savers are likely to benefit from higher returns. "The odds are, yes, we will see deposit rates continue to rise." But as ABC business reporter Adelaide Miller reported, Australians with billions in savings could be missing out on the benefits of rising rates if they're in the wrong account or fail to meet bonus rate conditions. Canstar found higher rates were often restricted to select products with strict requirements, with customers otherwise earning a base rate as low as 0.10 per cent. Other loans Read more Read more Car loans and personal loans can be affected by increases in the cash rate. But it all comes down to what type of loan you have. Australians collectively borrowed about $4.7 billion in fixed-term personal loans for road vehicles in the three months to June 2026, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics. These loans would not be affected by the cash rate until the fixed-rate period ended. For those on a variable rate however, Dr Oliver says banks may not necessarily hike rates by the full 0.25 per cent, but "the odds are they'll probably go up over time as well". Dr Mardiasmo says it also depends on who you have a car loan with: bank, car dealer, or the manufacturer themselves, and how each of those are structured. So the bottom line is check in with your finance provider.

When will we see rate cuts?

We don't know.

But the four major banks have their theories.

At this moment in time, Westpac, NAB and Commonwealth Bank economists predict we may see cuts from August 2027.

ANZ is a little more pessimistic, predicting the first rate cut could be in November.

The RBA will deliver its last cash rate decision for the year on Tuesday, December 8.

title: RBA lifts interest rates to highest level in 18 years to try to dampen inflation
text:
The Reserve Bank has lifted interest rates to their highest level in 18 years, while acknowledging it will take much longer to drag inflation down than it was expecting a few months ago.

It has increased rates by 0.25 percentage points, which lifts the cash rate target to 4.85 per cent, up from 4.60 per cent.

The cash rate has not been this high in Australia since late 2008. It is the fifth time the bank has lifted rates in 2026.

The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy RBA officials argue the hit to borrowers' income isn't the main way rate rises lower inflation. But they often omit a key fact.

The RBA board's decision to lift rates was not unanimous.

Six members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent, while three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent.

The majority decision will be another blow to households with mortgages.

But individuals who have high-interest savings accounts will see their savings accruing more interest after today's decision, if their bank applies higher rates to their accounts.

In a statement, the RBA board said inflation was now forecast to remain high throughout much of 2027 and was not expected to fall below 3 per cent until late 2027, which is "around three quarters later than previously forecast".

"This presents upside risks to inflation expectations," it said.

In recent weeks, RBA officials have been signalling their intention to lift rates at today's meeting, arguing that they can not afford to see peoples' inflation expectations drift higher.

The RBA wants annual inflation in consumer prices to be around 2.5 per cent on average over the cycle.

"There is an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that maybe 3 to 3.5 per cent is the new normal [for inflation]," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser warned last month.

"That is the central banker's nightmare. We can't allow expectations to shift away from the target," he said.

It takes between 12 and 18 months for a change in interest rates to flow completely through the economy, so we will not know what total impact this rate hike will have on economic activity until 2028.

Economy slowing, house prices falling, unemployment rising

The RBA Monetary Policy Board said the cumulative rate hikes this year have tightened financial conditions in Australia.

It says the economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly this year, and the unemployment rate has risen.

Why housing's the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds.

Its new economic forecasts see growth in output slowing even further over the coming year, which is expected to reduce capacity pressures and help return inflation to target.

It says employment is expected to keep growing, but the unemployment rate is projected to rise by more than expected.

In August, it was forecasting the unemployment rate to average 4.8 per cent in the December quarter of 2028, but now it was forecasting it to average 5.1 per cent in that period.

The unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent.

But the RBA board has also acknowledged that there continue to be "heightened uncertainties" about the outlook for inflation and the economy.

"The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast," it warned.

"Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation.

"A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia.

"To date, however, growth in Australia's major trading partners has been stronger than expected, as the boost from AI-related investment has outweighed the adverse effects of the Middle East conflict," it said.

Is the RBA pushing the economy into recession?

In her post-meeting press conference, RBA governor Michele Bullock left the door open for more rate increases.

She was then asked if the RBA was risking pushing Australia's economy into recession with more rate hikes.

The RBA and the inflation myth The Reserve Bank doesn't want consumer prices to come down, but to rise more slowly. It's a common misunderstanding that the ABS is partly responsible for.

"I want to be absolutely clear here," Bullock replied.

"The board's dual mandate is still in play here. We are not looking to tip the economy into recession if we can avoid it.

"But we do need to get inflation down, and we do have excess demand at the moment, so that is the key."

She said the RBA's new central forecast did not see Australia's economy falling into recession, but it did see economic growth slowing "markedly".

"It shows that inflation is quite sluggish, and I think that is going to … make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer, [and] their spending can't grow very quickly because their incomes aren't growing very quickly.

"This is a manifestation of lack of productivity growth and the fact that we've had this massive supply shock imposed upon us and we're all poorer," she said.

Are more rate hikes coming?

Some economists say the RBA may lift rates once more.

"Will a 4.85 per cent cash rate be enough? Sadly, it's still hard to be definitive at this point," BetaShares economist David Bassanese said.

"In fact, two further rate hikes in the first half of next year can't be ruled out to ensure a decent slowing in domestic demand and containment of inflation expectations.

"My base case is the RBA will raise rates again in February 2027.

"At the least, having now raised rates in both September and November, the RBA will likely feel able to leave rates on hold at the last policy meeting of the year next month, offering under-pressure households at least a Christmas reprieve," he said.

Share your experience with the housing market ABC News wants to hear your housing journey to better understand how the changing market is affecting your decisions.

EY chief economist Cherelle Murphy says the RBA is likely to take a wait-and-see approach over summer to allow the impact of the recent hikes to flow through the economy.

"With the cash rate at its highest level in almost two decades, it is likely that policy is sufficiently restrictive to return inflation sustainably to target," she said.

"But further increases in rates are possible, if the board thinks the tightening in conditions are unable to get inflation back to target in a reasonable time frame."

title: This Samoan superman is the World Cup's greatest comeback story
text:
As he prepares to lead his nation into a World Cup semifinal against Australia, sometimes Ronald Volkman still can't believe this is happening.

He'd have settled for one NRL game this year with Parramatta and after what he's been through, that really would have been enough.

But instead the best season of his budding career will continue when he lines up for Samoa against the Kangaroos with a World Cup final berth up for grabs, standing on the shoulders of giants with the whole rugby league world watching.

It still feels more like a fantasy than a reality for the 24-year-old, even as he's living it.

"I didn't see myself playing NRL and I didn't see myself playing for my country, in a World Cup, on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"I grew up watching this, I'm still pinching myself that I got to get on these fields.

Ronald Volkman will start in the halves for Samoa against Australia this weekend. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"The players in this team, you look left, you look right, you see guns. It gives you so much confidence in what you can do and that you can take it to the next level."

It has been a long journey. It was only a few years back that Volkman thought his football career was over.

Bad shoulder and hip injuries in 2023 scuppered a move from the Warriors to St George Illawarra the following season, sending Volkman to rock bottom in a full year out of the sport.

The physical pain was such that Volkman could barely move and without the game he loved he lost his way.

He stopped training and put on weight. He didn't know himself and when he was out and about, he'd pull his hood up so nobody would know him.

Mates would reached out to support him, but Volkman often ignored them, trapped in a downward spiral with a heart set on suffering, haunted by football dreams he could barely remember.

At his lowest depths, he leant on the things that mattered most to him.

Ronald Volkman's career and life fell apart after he left the Warriors. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"A big one for me was my faith. I fell down to that faith, my God, my loved ones, my family and my partner family," Volkman said.

"They were there for me during those tough times and it'd be slack for me not to take the opportunity I've had this year and showcase my talent, not for myself but for my loved ones.

"They've been through it as much as I have."

There's a lot of loved ones to repay.

Volkman is one of eight siblings and Samoan on both sides of the family. Growing up they'd go back to the islands every second year.

His father, Tas, wept tears of joy when his son debuted for the Warriors in 2022 and did so again when Volkman made his rugby league return in a pre-season trial for Parramatta last year.

Volkman did the same during the Samoan anthem on Sunday night but Emeline, Tas's mother, doesn't give as much away.

She still lives in Samoa, in a village called Vaitele Tai in the western outskirts of Apia, where she watched her grandson come on against Tonga and score a key try.

Loading Instagram content

Volkman played the final 27 minutes after Chanel Harris-Tavita strained his hamstring while kicking for goal, sparking a Samoan revival that just fell short despite the Toa outscoring Tonga four tries to three.

"I got rattled in the ribs early and struggled to breathe for about five minutes, but it's so good to be out there with my usos (brothers)," Volkman said.

"The first thing I thought was about Chanel. You never want to see a teammate go down like that and to me the way to honour him, to show respect, was to get on and do a job.

"He did a pretty good job for the majority of the game and it made my job easy."

Ronald Volkman has rebuilt his NRL career with Parramatta this year. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Volkman's play — the sharp feet, quick hands, a nose for the tryline and a big shot on Tongan backrower Siua Wong — would have been familiar to any Parramatta fans in the record-breaking crowd.

He made his NRL return for the Eels last year and just getting back at all and having his shoulder hold up was a blessing, even if they lost the two games by a combined total of 88-24.

This season, with the highly-rated Jonah Pezet arriving for one year, Volkman didn't expect to play any first grade.

But instead he relieved the injured Pezet in Round 6 and never looked back, playing every game for the rest of the season and signing a new two-year deal with the Eels in September.

He finished the year a blue and gold fan favourite, with Volkamania running wild among the Parramatta faithful.

In 2027 he'll act as a back-up to Mitchell Moses and Jarome Luai, but the latter has already had an impact on Volkman through Samoa camp.

"He's given me confidence to do what I do," Volkman said.

"The way he trains and prepares himself during the week is relentless.

"He's such a competitor but that's all I can say, because if he hears this he'll think I love him."

Tonga and Samoa can be Origin for the new century The scale and spectacle of Tonga's Rugby League World Cup win over Samoa was not just an instant classic, it proved a demand for this clash that rugby league must find a way to supply.

But before Volkman and Luai are club teammates they will be brothers in arms against Australia, starting in the halves together as the masters of Samoa's chaos.

A win over the Kangaroos would be a glittering prize at any time but with a World Cup final berth on the line the stakes are even higher it shapes as the biggest night of Volkman's career.

It would be Samoa's second and Volkman remembers watching the first four years ago and dreaming of being a part of it. Now, against all odds, that dream is real and the best could still be yet to come.

"I'd just started my first pre-season with the Warriors and it was mind-blowing, to see Samoa on the biggest stage," Volkman said.

"We have the chance to do it again next week, so let's do it. I can't wait."

Recreational fishers will be able to fish for species including snapper and dhufish off the Perth, Mid West and South West coasts when a controversial ban lifts in September next year, but when they drop a line will be highly restricted to winter months under changes flagged in an inquiry into the ban on Tuesday. Late last year, the Cook government indefinitely banned commercial demersal fishing from Augusta to Kalbarri and demersal trawling in the Pilbara to tackle low stocks of beloved WA species. Recreational demersal fishing in the “West Coast bioregion” from the South West to Kalbarri was banned until Spring 2027. The demersal fishing ban is facing an inquiry. Getty Images Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development top brass faced an Environment and Public Affairs committee inquiry into the ban on Tuesday, where one Fisheries boss revealed what recreational fishing of the popular species would look like after the ban. In response to a question from committee chair Sandra Carr about what rules would apply to recreational demersal fishing beyond September 2027, Fisheries and Aquaculture executive director Nathan Harrison said: “It cannot go back to the way that it was.”

Advertisement

“If fishing is going to commence for the recreational sector, the critical discussion then becomes around what is the sustainable benchmark that you could apply to the recreational fishery to allow that fishery to continue to recover,” he said. Harrison said before the ban, the commercial catch in the West Coast bioregion was between 220 and 240 tonnes of fish, while the recreational sector was catching around 220 tonnes as well. He said the total tonnage of fish being caught needed to be less than 100 tonnes annually to ensure the species continued to recover, but he understood that would be challenging given there were 130,000 licensed recreational fishers in the state – and 30,000 of those caught demersal fish. “When you look at 30,000 people, 100 tons is actually not many fish,” he said. Harrison flagged seasonal closures – likely in the warmer months – would be used to keep this catch down.

Advertisement

Related Article Fishing ‘I’ve basically annoyed everyone’: WA minister’s anger over fishing ban threats “The window of fishing that’s available to the recreational sector when it does reopen would have to be fairly small to allow that catch of 100 tons,” he said. “To try and avoid the key spawning times for dhufish and pink snapper, which traditionally spawn over the summer months … you may have a limited winter fishery to manage that catch to 100 tons.” Harrison also reiterated there would be mandatory reporting for the recreational sector requiring fishers to report their catch as soon as they got back to the boat ramp. The ban was met with backlash from the commercial fishing sector, which questioned the science behind the ban, saying anecdotally it did not match what they were seeing on the water.

Advertisement

Commercial fishers also criticised the compensation on offer from government for their licenses, which the Cook Government budgeted $20 million for. During the inquiry, the committee heard 13 commercial fishers had negotiated a deal with the government to buy back their licenses, 13 more negotiations were under way, and 27 more had opted to launch a class action against the government. About $6 million of the fund has been spent so far. The issue has resulted in high-profile protests from commercial fishers like East Bunbury man Brendan Bardowski, 37, who was fined for dumping shark heads and fish guts outside WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis’ electoral office in December. In her evidence to the committee, which was established in February this year, director general Heather Brayford lamented the social media discourse over the ban, warning the evidence her team provided would likely be “twisted” on social media and used to attack staff members.

Advertisement

“Based on what we’ve seen, today, it’s highly likely that the aspects of our evidence today may find their way to Facebook or other platforms, and will be twisted and turned by those seeking to discredit the department and, in some cases, to personally attack the individual staff members,” she said. Harrison reiterated his agency was concerned about the total biomass of demersal fish off the WA coast. Biomass is an estimation of the total weight of fish in an ecosystem and Harrison said pink snapper was 20 per cent of its original biomass and Dhufish was lower than along some parts of the WA coastline. He said the problem was there were no old fish left. “We have aged over 60,000 fish … the stock assessment is showing that we have actually no old fish left in the population,” he said.

Advertisement

“So you don’t get the same number of juvenile fish joining the fishery each year. “So that’s something that adds to that risk around that assessment in relation to commercial scale fishing.” The department revealed it was using drone trials to ensure the ban was being complied with and fisheries offices had about 20,000 interactions with fishers.

It took all of 15 minutes to set up the portable stage and catwalk on which his band, and occasionally he, played, and the set itself lasted only about the same. But just before the Melbourne Cup was run Robbie Williams delivered a typically knockout set that is guaranteed to linger for years in the memory of those who were there to witness it.

No stranger to marquee events, Williams knows how to package up the hits and memories amassed over three decades in the business into a tight package made for the camera. But in no way did he shortchange the punters who were actually there at Flemington.

Robbie Williams in full flight before the big race. Getty Images

With his 10-strong band already on the hastily erected — and just as hastily dismantled afterwards — stage, he entered the Mounting Yard looking every bit the thoroughbred he is. I’m in the middle of mountains of post-holiday laundry when my dearly beloved calls me so insistently I assume he’s having a medical episode. Midway down the stairs, arms full of unfolded undies and unpaired socks, I hear what he’s actually saying. Come talk to this woman. She’s doorknocking for NSW Labor. Premier, your approach to discipline isn’t working. It never works Oscar Colman She’s charming. A councillor in another area. But I am so embarrassed to have to confess this, I was utterly unprepared. I have a few issues with Chris Minns and here was a willing pair of ears who would take important policy critiques from my mouth to God’s ear. Or at least to the premier. But when she asked if I had any problems, I lied. My bloke had a few words to say about the way protesters had been treated. But me? Reliably outspoken and opinionated ole me? Nothing. It was like I had brain freeze.

Advertisement

I never want you to be the dud I was on that occasion, so here’s my list. Turns out that doorknockers don’t really want to know what you think in any fine-grained way. You’re just one ageing grandma with an opinion. Phoebe Hayman, researcher at La Trobe University and an expert on doorknocking, says the practice is more about spreading the vibe, the warmth, the personal contact. Yeah OK, but no thanks. I have so much warmth I’m melting. Related Article Healthcare Doctors fear Catholic takeover of NSW hospitals will usher in ‘religious doctrine’ So what should I have said? Chris Minns, here are (*not quite) 10 things I hate about you. Please fix them stat. How – on God’s green Earth – are we letting Catholic health into more hospitals in this state? Now, in my humble view which I couldn’t articulate with an armful of laundry, you can’t have hospitals which don’t offer essential services. Calvary Health Care follows Catholic Health Australia’s Code of Ethical Standards. That bans contraception, termination of pregnancy, IVF services and voluntary assisted dying. We do not need one more hospital with limited services in this state. Not one. Women already struggle with abortion access. Why make it worse?

Advertisement

Plus, my goodness, Chris, have you been to emergency with a fevered kid lately? Where are the doctors and nurses? More of them, please, urgently. You are meant to be admitted, discharged or transferred from the emergency within four hours. Of all the things that never happen, this never happens the most. Related Article Healthcare Revealed: The Sydney hospital where one in 10 patients waits more than 43 hours for a bed Let me help you be a better premier. You’re a bit removed from what happens in public schools. Here’s what I see. Not enough permanent staff to do the job. Schools are not just about putting teachers in front of classes. They are also about devising programs to support every kid in the place. It’s about sport and drama and music and art and in-class support for kids who need it. It’s about management and money and plans and parents, the bullies, the devastated, the proud. I sit in a public school playground three mornings a week. The principal is out there doing the doing with staff and parents. And, ahem, with grandparents who’ve forgotten the day of the school assemblies where their adorable eldest grandchild is getting an award. Think that’s excess to requirements? I was on public school P&Cs for 10 straight years. That’s how you build communities that choose public education.

Advertisement

Turns out, I was grateful to have my heroic husband there to save me on the day of the doorknock. The civil liberties thing is trash in this state. Laws rushed through. Will those laws protect a single Jew from antisemitism? I doubt that so much. Raging antisemitism has existed in this country for as long as I’ve been alive. Education works. Police beating the crap out of protesters does not. Loading There are more people in jail in NSW under a Labor government than there were under a Liberal government. Your approach to discipline isn’t working. It never works. Want fewer kids in jail? Fund the youth sector so we can interrupt the school-to-prison pipelines. Those youth hubs won’t build or staff themselves. Four government inquiries have recommended early intervention. Four. Do it. Just read the parliamentary inquiry into loneliness and sort this out. And would it be remotely possible for you to distance yourself from the mining lobby? Even a few metres? The environment – and therefore the entirety of NSW – would be grateful. Look, I could go on, but Hayman tells me that we need to get all our neighbours to say more or less the same thing to make an impact. Do that. Practice makes perfect.

title: RBA's Cup Day call takes rates to 18-year high; board divided over decision — as it happened
text:
The RBA governor is talking

RBA governor Michele Bullock says she knows this was not the news many Australians wanted, but "it's what's needed to get inflation down".

"Inflation is too high and our forecasts suggest it will stay higher for longer," she said at a press conference.

"Part of the reason for inflation staying higher for longer is global oil prices. However, I want to be very clear that we are not tightening monetary policy because of the direct impact of oil prices on inflation."

She noted that rate hikes began before the start of the war in Iran.

"Monetary policy cannot impact global oil prices. Rather, the tightening in monetary policy is to address domestic capacity pressures. These were evident before the rise in oil prices, which is why the board started to increase the cash rate in February this year."

"We now think that those pressures were greater and contributed more to inflation than we judged before."

She said that Australians with mortgages are not the only ones dealing with the higher cost of living.

"I understand that today's decision is going to be difficult for Australians with mortgages, many of whom are already managing large repayments, but households with mortgages are not the only Australians doing it tough," she said.

"If high inflation were allowed to become entrenched, interest rates would ultimately need to stay higher for longer, with greater risks for economic growth and jobs."

— Josie Harvey

title: UK adventurer embraces mother after completing 28-year trek around the world
text:
In brief Bushby set out from Chile in 1998 and walked 50,000km across four continents and 30 countries to get home.

The 57-year-old said he expects to struggle with the ups and downs other adventurers have experienced after long journeys.

British adventurer Karl Bushby enjoyed an emotional reunion with his mother and family on Monday as he arrived back home after a 28-year, 50,000-km trek from South America, crossing four continents on foot.

Cheers erupted as the 57-year-old former paratrooper was greeted in the street outside his mother's house in the north-eastern UK port city of Hull.

Bushby, who set off on his odyssey from Chile in 1998, had two golden rules for his journey — avoid all forms of transport to advance and not return until he completed his challenge.

He was met in the centre of Hull by a crowd of up to 1,000 cheering people before being reunited with his mother, Angela, 36-year-old son Adam and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.

Speaking after the reunion, Bushby paid tribute to the kindness of the strangers he had met, from hotel owners to the "poorest of the poor" who had given him bowls of rice and something to drink along the way.

"And that would happen throughout the world," he said, adding that the world had been his "support network".

'Indiana Jones' moments

The route back to his home city has taken him across the Americas, across the frozen Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia, and then through parts of Central Asia and Europe, covering jungles, mountains, and deserts.

The journey had been full of logistical headaches and scary "Indiana Jones" and "I think I'm going to die moments", he told reporters.

Bushby had already been applauded on Sunday as he crossed the iconic Humber Bridge near Hull in thick mist, ahead of his final push into the city centre and then on to his mother's home where he grew up.

Karl Bushby in Nevada in the United States in 2003. Source: PA / tiktok.com/@karlcbushby

"So many people have followed Karl on his epic journey. We have all felt inspired by his spirit, tenacity and dogged determination," Hull mayor Maria Coward said ahead of his arrival.

"It's quite emotional. I'm proud of him and what he's done. What an achievement," neighbour Laura Chaplin, 47, told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency as he returned home.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesperson said it was "an extraordinary achievement and the prime minister welcomes him back to the UK".

Challenges met

Bushby began his adventure aged 29, after his marriage broke down and his wife returned to Northern Ireland with their son.

He was forced to pause the journey several times, including when Moscow refused him a visa. The 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic caused other hold-ups.

At those times, he stepped away from the journey, living notably at a base in Mexico, then once the situation had been resolved, he would resume from the exact spot where he had left off.

Erin Anderson, 28, a theatre marketing officer among the crowd in Hull, said she thought Bushby was "amazing".

"I've been following him for the last eight years. He's been walking for as long as I've been alive. It's brilliant."

What's next for Bushby?

Bushby swam across the Channel from France in early October to return to the UK.

Legendary German filmmaker Werner Herzog and a film crew accompanied Bushby on his homecoming, making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled Walk of Life.

The production company behind the film has been supporting Bushby's progress for the past 16 years, providing financial and logistical assistance.

Bushby said he would now be focusing on the documentary, as well as writing a book and adjusting back to normal life.

James Bushby was mobbed by well-wishers as he arrived in Hull after his 28-year trek. Source: EPA / Adam Vaughan

"I'm still in that shocked phase," he told AFP. "Over the last few days it's been the last time I've been camping in my tent ... last time spending all day on the road.

"Each one of those has been an emotional event and then walking down my childhood street into my childhood home with mother (there), that's been quite something," he said.

He added that he still had the drive for adventure but ruled out any more big walks.

"I think I'm hanging my boots up — 28 years is a good run."

title: What number should your interest rate have in front of it?
text:
IN BRIEF It's widely anticipated the RBA will raise the rate to 4.85 per cent, a fifth rise in 2026.

Experts say it's worth speaking with your bank, or shopping around for better options.

Homeowners could save big by negotiating or refinancing their mortgages, experts say, as the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) prepares to decide on its cash rate on Tuesday.

It's widely anticipated the RBA will raise the rate from 4.60 per cent to 4.85 per cent. If it does, it will be the fifth rate rise of 2026, and sent interest rates to an 18-year high.

For those on variable interest rates, another hike would likely add 0.25 percentage points to their repayments, as the major banks have historically passed on the rate in full after RBA announcements.

But while a rate rise could increase mortgage pain for borrowers, it could also create an opportunity for people to negotiate their loan.

Sally Tindall is the head of data analytics at financial comparison site Canstar. She told SBS News that the best variable rate on offer was 5.89 per cent as of Tuesday morning.

"It's an important time to be talking to your bank," she said.

"Any kind of relief that you can get on an individual basis from your bank can help alleviate some of the pressure that the RBA is applying on you."

What is a good variable rate?

Mardy Chiah, an associate professor of finance at the University of Newcastle, told SBS News that a variable rate of around 6 per cent to 6.3 per cent for a maximum 80 per cent loan-to-value ratio (LVR) is competitive ahead of the RBA's decision.

An 80 per cent LVR means you are borrowing 80 per cent of a property's appraised value or purchase price, leaving you with a 20 per cent deposit or equity.

"If you're paying 6.5 per cent or more, it's worth shopping around or asking your bank for a better deal," he said.

Reducing your rate from 6.5 per cent to 6 per cent on a $500,000 mortgage could save you around $160 a month, or nearly $2,000 a year, assuming 30 years remaining, he explained.

Tindall said that the average variable rate sits at 6.49 per cent, so any loan at or under that figure is in the better half of loans.

A good home loan should also suit a borrower's circumstances, experts say.

Someone who values certainty might prefer a fixed interest rate, which keeps repayments stable for the fixed term. Others might prefer a variable rate, which can offer greater flexibility and the potential to benefit when rates fall.

Having a clear understanding of what you are paying for and the features attached to your loan is the most important thing.

When should borrowers negotiate or refinance?

One of the biggest mistakes borrowers can make is assuming their existing lender will automatically offer them its most competitive rate.

Banks and lenders regularly compete for new customers, so existing borrowers can sometimes end up paying more than people taking out a new mortgage.

"The bottom line is that loyalty doesn't always pay when it comes to mortgages," Chiah said.

"Banks may offer better rates to attract new customers, so existing borrowers shouldn't be afraid to ask for the same treatment."

It is also worth reviewing your loan when a fixed-rate period is about to expire, when your property has increased in value, or when you have paid down a substantial portion of your mortgage.

Barriers to refinancing

However, not everyone can refinance, as finding a new bank requires going through the institution's approval process.

A new lender won't necessarily approve a loan for someone who doesn't pass the checks and tests it puts you through.

"If you don't own 20 per cent of your home at today's values, a lender may not take you on. Some borrowers may also fail to pass serviceability tests," Tindall from Canstar explained.

Tindall described not being able to find a new bank as "mortgage prison" but said it's still worth looking at refinancing, as it could put pressure on your current bank to come to the table.

What could variable rates be after a rate hike?

An interest rate of 4.85 per cent would see any variable rate starting with a 5 "dead and buried", Tindall said.

The average variable rate would rise to 6.74 per cent in line with the RBA rise.

But there would still be some good options available, she predicted.

"The lowest variable rate could still sit below 6.20 per cent, it'll be interesting to see what the lower-cost lenders do in terms of their rates."

title: House prices are falling across Australia. But not in these places
text:
In Brief Regional home prices rose 3.1 per cent over the year, even as national values continued to fall.

The Barossa, outback SA and WA's Wheatbelt have seen the biggest increases over the year.

House prices are falling across Australia, but some regional areas are still seeing double-digit growth.

Australia's housing downturn has stretched into its seventh straight month, with national home prices falling 0.3 per cent in October.

The latest REA Group Home Price Report shows home values are now 4.3 per cent below their March peak and 1.9 per cent lower than a year ago, as higher interest rates continue to weigh on borrowing power and buyer demand.

Capital cities are leading the decline, now 5.4 per cent below their peak and 3.7 per cent lower than a year ago.

But the downturn isn't playing out evenly across the country.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While headline figures point to a broad slowdown, some regional markets continue to record strong annual growth, even as buyers pull back elsewhere.

"There's quite a bit of diversity under the headline numbers," Tim Lawless, research director at property analytics firm Cotality, told SBS News.

READ MORE Ninth life: What 30 years of housing downturns can tell us about this one

Regional home prices fell just 0.1 per cent in October and remain 3.1 per cent higher than a year ago, outperforming capital city markets despite the broader slowdown.

While regional markets have not escaped the downturn entirely, they have generally held up better than the capitals, said REA Group senior economist Eleanor Creagh.

"Regional areas in general have so far been more resilient than the capital city markets," Creagh told SBS News.

Capital cities are leading the housing drop, now 5.4 per cent below their peak and 3.7 per cent lower than a year ago. Source: SBS News

The regional hotspots bucking the trend

Several of the regions posting the largest price increases are concentrated in SA and WA.

The Barossa, Yorke and Mid North region in SA topped the annual growth rankings, with prices up 12.3 per cent over the past year.

It was followed by outback SA (11.65 per cent), outback WA (11.22 per cent) and WA's Wheatbelt region (11.02 per cent).

Tasmania's Launceston and North East region rounded out the top five, recording annual growth of 10.74 per cent.

Creagh said many of the best-performing regions shared a common advantage: affordability.

Rural regions across South Australia and Western Australia have seen some of the largest year on year price increases. Source: SBS News

"They're largely regional areas that continue to really benefit from comparative affordability advantages," Creagh said.

She pointed to regional SA, where median home values sit around $530,000, significantly lower than many regional NSW markets that have seen steeper declines.

That affordability buffer has become increasingly important as interest rates have climbed and borrowing power has fallen.

Regional markets continue to outperform

The difference between city and regional markets is stark over longer timeframes.

Regional home prices have risen 3.1 per cent over the past year, 33.9 per cent over five years and 108.4 per cent over the past decade.

By comparison, capital city prices are down 3.7 per cent over the past year and have risen 16.4 per cent over five years and 56.6 per cent over 10 years.

Regional South Australia recorded the strongest annual growth among the states, with prices rising 10.2 per cent over the year.

Western Australia followed at 8.9 per cent and Tasmania at 8.7 per cent.

Regional home prices have risen 3.1 per cent over the past year, 33.9 per cent over five years and 108.4 per cent over the past decade. Source: SBS News

Queensland recorded annual growth of 3.3 per cent, while the Northern Territory (2.4 per cent), Victoria (1.6 per cent) and NSW (1.4 per cent) posted more modest gains.

Over five years, regional WA and SA have been Australia's standout performers, with prices increasing 85.1 per cent and 84.6 per cent respectively.

Why are prices still rising?

Economists say the same factors driving prices lower nationally are helping support demand in some regional markets.

Lawless from Cotality described the current correction as "very much a demand-driven downturn", with higher borrowing costs reducing what many buyers can afford.

As household budgets come under pressure, buyers are increasingly adjusting their expectations and looking at cheaper locations.

READ MORE Why Australia's richest suburbs could be a warning for every homeowner

Creagh said many prospective buyers had effectively been pushed down the property ladder.

"We know that as interest rates have risen substantially, maximum borrowing capacities for potential buyers have also reduced substantially," she said.

"More affordable regions and property types remain an option for a broader pool of buyers, so are less impacted by interest rate rises."

Lawless said affordability pressures have become one of the dominant forces shaping the market.

"Affordability and serviceability challenges are just pushing more demand towards lower price points," he said.

'A double-edged sword'

While many regional areas are still recording growth, Creagh cautioned they are not immune from broader housing market pressures.

"High mortgage repayments and reduced purchasing power are also weighing on demand in many regional areas, but relative affordability, local conditions, stock on the market, and differing demand conditions in some regional areas mean there's much more resilience there than in capital cities."

The trend does not necessarily mean housing has become more affordable.

"Higher interest rates have reduced how much they can borrow, and the decline in home prices hasn't been enough to offset that," Creagh said.

"Better buying conditions don't mean better affordability."

— With additional reporting by Hannah Kwon.
